### 12.6 Migration safety conclusion

The current EF model matches the committed snapshot, the canonical submission-state migration includes an explicit legacy backfill, the Internal Audit migration contains only its two governed tables, the original official-report migration contains only its template/generation tables and constraints/indexes, the report-family migration adds only the two class columns plus bounded constraints, the asynchronous-report migration contains only its governed schedule/job tables and relationships, the SDBIP-layer migration is additive while preserving nullable historic target rows for controlled reconciliation, the global-reference migration contains only its two masters and two availability mappings, the strategic-planning migration contains only its five masters and five optional relationship tables, the KPI-classification migration adds fourteen nullable references with deterministic unique-match backfill before restricted FK creation, the governed-budget migration adds four masters/junction tables plus two nullable target references with conservative referenced-value backfill before restricted target FK creation, the governed-performance-classification migration adds four masters plus seven nullable target references with per-tenant distinct-value backfill before restricted FK creation, the KPI-unit migration adds one master plus two nullable target references with a preservation-oriented per-municipality copy/backfill before restricted composite target FKs, the Vote Number year-scope migration adds one nullable historical key with conservative linked-KPI/single-year reconciliation before its composite tenant/year FK and filtered unique index, the canonical OPMS Unit/Performance Direction migration adds two exact seeded masters plus three nullable historical relationships with deterministic known-enum backfill before restricted foreign keys, the target-template identity migration additively backfills four unique public identifiers before enforcing them, introduces SQL Server native `rowversion` concurrency and enforces one logical version number per template, the security-history identity migration additively backfills four unique public identifiers before enforcing them while adding native SQL Server `rowversion` to mutable scope and assignment histories, and the IDP secondary-identity migration additively backfills eleven unique public identifiers before enforcing them while adding native SQL Server `rowversion` to eight mutable secondary records. Ambiguous or absent legacy classifications, Vote Number years and unknown unit/direction values are deliberately not fabricated. Relational SQLite tests exercise the shared model; idempotent SQL Server scripts can be generated; and supplemental SQL Server 2025 Express LocalDB execution applied the entire chain and proved trusted constraints, filtered indexes, native rowversion advancement and DBCC integrity. These are useful pre-deployment controls, but they do not prove target-instance or production migration safety. The historical chain must still be applied both to a clean approved SQLEXPRESS database and to a production-shaped upgrade copy, followed by reconciliation of row counts/ownership/state, exact-instance concurrency/locking tests, rollback/transaction checks and backup/restore validation. Until that evidence exists, target SQL Server migration safety remains **Not Verifiable** and production deployment must not be approved.

The exact-instance qualification in the preceding historical-chain paragraph is superseded by section 11.521: the mandated clean `localhost\SQLEXPRESS` chain, native concurrency/constraints, rollback, cutover, representative load and checksum backup/isolated restore now pass. Migration safety remains unapproved only for an owner-approved production-shaped legacy copy and its real exception population, topology and cutover sign-off.

### 12.7 Release decision

The completed remediation closes the repository-implementable requirements identified by this assessment, including all required official report classes, durable generation/scheduling/distribution, version history, bounded production target selection, governed historical cutover consoles, provider-neutral cutover/performance/recovery harnesses, exact local SQL Server acceptance and complete applicable rendered route acceptance. The software implementation verdict is therefore **SUBSTANTIALLY COMPLIANT — EXTERNAL ACCEPTANCE REMAINS**. Release approval still requires execution/sign-off against a production-shaped legacy copy, physical compatibility-column retirement after owner approval, credential rotation, live federation, independent security testing, deployed performance/operations evidence, representative-user accessibility and formal UAT. Until those obligations are completed, the separate production decision remains **NOT PRODUCTION READY**.
